children: By Maxwell Zeff and Meghan Bobrowsky
SAN FRANCISICO — An OpenAI engineer visited a familiar conference room in one of the company's San Francisco office buildings last week — and peered behind a television set mounted to a wall.

Abdulrahman Alfozan had spent weeks scoping out the room, which could only be reserved by executives at the artificial-intelligence company and their assistants, federal prosecutors allege. The conference room was often used for leadership meetings, briefings with government officials and business partners as well as top-secret research and product discussions.
Alfozan, who had worked on OpenAI's product team for more than a year, planned to intercept what was said within its walls, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

The 35-year-old Saudi national is accused of wrapping a thumb-sized circuit board and microphone in toilet paper and inserting the device into the USB port on the back of the wall-mounted TV in late September.

After OpenAI found the hidden device, it alerted the Federal Bureau of Investigation and investigators placed a camera in the conference room. Last Monday, they captured footage prosecutors say shows Alfozan looking behind the TV.

The bug was one of two encrypted recording devices linked to Alfozan that prosecutors say were discovered in the office. The other was found in a bag that the suspect left unattended, later reported missing and went to retrieve from the company lost-and-found.
Attempts to reach Alfozan and to determine the identity of his lawyer were unsuccessful.

Silicon Valley companies have long warned employees about the risk that adversaries could try to steal their commercial secrets. The Justice Department's arrest underscores that threats often originate within a firm's own ranks.
Earlier this year, a former Google employee was indicted for stealing trade secrets related to the company's Pixel phones. And in 2022, a Twitter employee was found guilty of spying for Saudi Arabia.

That man, Ahmad Abouammo, passed on private user information associated with critics of the kingdom in exchange for hundreds of thousands of dollars, prosecutors said. Abouammo's lawyers said during the trial that he had simply been doing his job at Twitter and that the government hadn't met the burden of proof regarding allegations that he was involved in a scheme to feed information to Saudi officials.
Scoping things out
Alfozan, a foreign national, went to school in the U.S. and has been a legal permanent resident since September 2020.

OpenAI hired him in July 2025 after his multiyear stint at the San Francisco-based logistics startup Nash, which was backed by Andreessen Horowitz. Alfozan had worked previously at Meta Platforms for several years as a senior systems engineer, and held internships at Microsoft and SAP, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Alfozan is currently listed as a venture partner at the Saudi-based investment firm, Raed, according to its website and his LinkedIn. Nash, Microsoft and Raed didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Meta and SAP declined to comment.

Late this past summer, prosecutors allege, Alfozan began querying an internal AI tool for information about OpenAI buildings, meeting rooms and calendars. In mid-September, he made multiple queries about conference rooms, including "can you list today's meeting in this room" and "how about external partners, where would those usually meet."
An FBI agent wrote in an affidavit that the queries suggested he was researching where at OpenAI to place the first recording device.

Alfozan repeatedly scoped out the conference room where he would later place the recording device, the complaint alleges. Closed-circuit television footage inside the building captured him near the conference room — which he wasn't authorized to access — at least 10 times in September.

His spouse appeared to have helped him with the alleged surveillance attempt, the FBI agent wrote. A chatbot account associated with his spouse submitted prompts late last month about building a "continuous audio recorder," improving live listening and testing recording reliability, among other things.
Installing the device

Around Sept. 28, prosecutors say, Alfozan installed the bug — a Chinese-made circuit board device with "a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone" and a small memory card behind the TV. It was discovered in a security sweep about two days later.

OpenAI said it removed the device, closed the room, conducted additional security sweeps and contacted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to help analyze the device, reviewing forensic images of its storage and assessing changes in the underlying data.

Last Monday, the same day Alfozan was captured on video looking behind the TV, he left a bag unattended in a printer room that contained a second recording device. That device, "had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications," the FBI agent wrote.

The engineer retrieved his bag, which no longer contained the second recording device, the next afternoon. He asked about items he said were missing, including a credit card, about $500 cash and sunglasses, the FBI affidavit said. He didn't ask about the device.

OpenAI says that it worked with the FBI to time Alfozan's firing and arrest in order not to disrupt the investigation. It took gradual steps to restrict his access to systems and spaces. Alfozan was arrested Friday and charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications.
